title: A map of the course
description: Understand the course as one connected journey, from inductive definitions to interpreters and type inference.

title: Textbook · Complete contents
description: Follow all nine chapters in the original section order, with linked definitions, Mermaid thinking flows, and worked problems.

title: 1. Induction
description: Define sets and languages, then prove properties by following their construction rules.

title: 2. Functional Programming
description: Read OCaml, derive recursion, and solve the twelve exercises in section 2.4.

title: 2.4 Problems · Worked solutions
description: Derive each solution with a Mermaid thinking flow, worked OCaml code, and boundary checks.

title: 3. Variables and the Environment
description: Follow the textbook from syntax and environments to an executable interpreter.

title: 4. Defining and Calling Functions
description: Trace static and dynamic scope, build closures, and implement recursive procedures.

title: 5. Functional Language Fun
description: Combine lists, mutually recursive closures, output, and sequencing into a complete language.

title: 6. State Changes
description: Compare explicit and implicit references and solve both stateful interpreter tasks.

title: 7. Pointers and Memory Management
description: Follow records and pointers, then solve all four evaluator and garbage-collector tasks.

title: 8. Static Type Systems
description: Read typing rules, generate and solve equations, and implement the Fun extension.

title: 9. Lambda Calculus
description: Understand substitution and normal order, then build a reducer and translators.

title: Your OCaml workbench
description: Use the official OCaml environment and build a repeatable study loop.

title: Thinking in constructors
description: Turn inductive rules into data types, recursive functions, and structural proofs.

title: Reading and writing OCaml
description: Expressions, types, pattern matching, currying, and algebraic data types.

title: The recursive way of thinking
description: Derive recursion from the shape of data and use functions to express reusable patterns.

title: From rules to an interpreter
description: Read semantic judgments and turn them into a small executable language.

title: What a function remembers
description: Explain lexical scope by drawing the environment captured at function creation.

title: Names, scope, and recursive calls
description: Connect recursive closures, mutual recursion, free variables, and nameless representations.

title: When evaluation changes memory
description: Separate environments from stores and trace call-by-value versus call-by-reference.

title: Following the pointers
description: Reason about shared fields, heap reachability, and memory safety.

title: The work left to do
description: Make pending computation explicit and see why raising an exception discards frames.

title: Objects as state plus dispatch
description: Build the mental model for fields, method lookup, self, super, and inheritance.

title: Reason before running
description: Use typing judgments to rule out classes of runtime mistakes.

title: Turn types into equations
description: Generate constraints, solve them with substitutions, and understand the occurs check.

title: One definition, many types
description: Generalize only independent type variables and instantiate a scheme freshly at each use.

title: When one type can stand for another
description: Understand substitution, function variance, and safe method overriding.

title: The small language underneath
description: Connect substitution, evaluation strategies, encodings, and fixed points.

title: Lecture cheat sheets · 0–20
description: Review each lecture’s focus, formulas, syntax, reasoning flow, textbook connection, and homework.

title: L0 · Course overview
description: Learn language concepts by defining a small language and implementing its interpreter. OCaml is the implementation tool; the interpreted language is a separate object of study.

title: L1 · Inductive definitions I
description: Define an infinite set using finite base and construction rules, with no extra elements.

title: L2 · Inductive definitions II
description: The shape of a datatype determines the cases of its recursive functions and structural proofs.

title: L3 · Basics of OCaml
description: Read OCaml as expressions built from bindings, functions, patterns, and typed values.

title: L4 · Recursion and higher-order programming
description: Solve a smaller instance, then combine its result; abstract repeated traversal with functions.

title: L5 · Expressions and environments
description: Translate each evaluation rule into a matching AST case and keep the environment explicit.

title: L6 · Procedures and recursive closures
description: A lexical procedure carries the environment where it was defined; a call extends that saved environment.

title: L7 · Lexical addresses and nameless programs
description: Resolve a variable to its binder statically and replace names with positions.

title: L8 · State and parameter passing
description: Separate the binding map from mutable memory and carry the updated store through every evaluation step.

title: L9 · Records, pointers, and garbage collection
description: Follow locations through structured values and distinguish unreachable memory from memory that merely looks unused.

title: L10 · Exceptions and continuations
description: Make pending computation explicit so a raised exception can discard frames up to the nearest handler.

title: L11 · Classes and objects
description: An object combines mutable field locations with a class identity used for method lookup.

title: L12 · Why static types?
description: Use a computable static approximation to prevent a specified class of runtime type errors.

title: L13 · Designing typing rules
description: Build typing derivations using a type environment instead of executing the program.

title: L14 · Manual type annotations
description: Explicit procedure annotations make syntax-directed checking possible without guessing parameter types.

title: L15 · Type inference I: the idea
description: Infer unknown types from how expressions are used, by turning typing rules into equations.

title: L16 · Type inference II: constraint generation
description: Define V(Γ,e,t) to generate the equalities required for expression e to have target type t.

title: L17 · Type inference III: unification
description: Solve type equations by substitution, decomposition, mismatch rejection, and the occurs check.

title: L18 · Let-polymorphism
description: Generalize independent type variables at let bindings and instantiate them freshly at each use.

title: L19 · Typed objects and subtyping
description: Check class programs using safe substitutability, with contravariant method inputs and covariant outputs.

title: L20 · Lambda calculus
description: Understand functions and application as a small core, then make binding and reduction strategy precise.

title: Definitions → homework
description: Find the exact definitions, chapters, and source pages needed for each assignment.

title: HW1 · Learn to think recursively
description: Problem-by-problem strategies, connections, and boundary tests for functional programming.

title: HW2 · Build the ML− interpreter
description: A staged implementation guide for lists, closures, recursive procedures, and undefined semantics.

title: HW3 · Build the B interpreter
description: A memory-aware implementation guide for variables, records, loops, and parameter passing.

title: HW4 · Build the type checker
description: A precise design guide for a sound checker, including underspecified cases in the assignment.

title: Syntax · Meaning and sources
description: Connect OCaml tokens, language syntax, evaluation judgments, and type notation to definitions and source pages.

title: Notation & glossary
description: Translate mathematical notation into the data and functions you implement in OCaml.

title: Course sources & reading list
description: All course PDF links, local download status, source discrepancies, and reading references.
